component-address-poisoning-intro-1: Ethereum addresses are 40 random-looking characters, and almost nobody reads all of them. People check the first few and the last few, then copy the address from their own transaction history.
component-address-poisoning-intro-2: Scammers rely on this. Transaction history is public, so they can see who you pay. They generate an address that starts and ends like your contact's, then send you a worthless transfer from it, or make a zero-value transfer look like it came from you. It lands in your history right next to the real one. This is called address poisoning.
component-address-poisoning-task: You owe your friend Sam for the cinema, so you open your wallet's history to copy Sam's address. Which row would you copy it from?
component-address-poisoning-idle: Pick the row you'd copy Sam's address from.
component-address-poisoning-wrong-reason: It was a zero-value transfer the scammer made look like it came from you.
It was a tiny deposit from the scammer's lookalike address.
component-address-poisoning-wrong-conseq: Your payment went to the scammer. Ethereum transfers can't be reversed.
component-address-poisoning-wrong-timing: Both fakes arrived within minutes of your real payment, so they sat at the top of your history.
component-address-poisoning-right: Right this time. Now imagine doing it on your phone, late at night, for the hundredth time.
component-address-poisoning-right-explai: The other rows were fakes. Compare the middle characters above: that's the only part that differs.
component-address-poisoning-right-once: The trick only has to work once.
component-address-poisoning-caption: Sample data. Wallets shorten addresses to the first and last few characters, and so do most people's eyes.
component-address-poisoning-avoid-item-1: Check the whole address before you send, including the middle, not only the start and end.
component-address-poisoning-avoid-item-2: Save the people you pay in your wallet's address book, or use an <glossary>ENS</glossary> name you've confirmed with them.
component-address-poisoning-avoid-item-3: Don't copy addresses from your transaction history. Unexpected tiny or zero-value transfers there are a warning sign.
component-address-poisoning-record-wbtc: Someone copied a poisoned address and sent 1,155 wrapped bitcoin, worth about 68 million US dollars, to a scammer. The fake matched the first four and last six characters of the address they meant to use. After public negotiations, the attacker sent back almost all of its value, in ETH, about a week later.
component-address-poisoning-record-study: Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University measured two years of address poisoning on Ethereum and BNB Smart Chain. They counted 270 million attempts aimed at 17 million victims. At least 6,633 attempts worked, costing victims at least 83.8 million US dollars.
component-address-poisoning-source-study: Tsuchiya et al., "Blockchain Address Poisoning", USENIX Security 2025
